background.definition: Acute bronchitis is a clinical diagnosis, and is an acute lower respiratory tract infection with cough as the predominant symptom, with or without sputum production, usually lasting 10 days to 3 weeks. Patients will not have clinical or radiographic evidence of pneumonia, and will not have the common cold, acute asthma exacerbation, or an exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).

list.listitem: Fifty per 1000 people per year.
Ten ambulatory visits per 1000 people per year.
Ten million office visits per year.
Respiratory viruses (90%) including influenza B, influenza A, parainfluenza, and respiratory syncytial virus.
Bacterial causes (<10%) include Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia pneumoniae, Bordetella pertussis, and Bordetella parapertussis.

An observational study of 618 adults with acute LRTI and PCR for 46 pathogens found at least one viral potential pathogen in 17%, one or more bacterial pathogens in 34%, a mix of viral and bacterial pathogens in 27%, and no detection in the remainder. The most common potential bacterial pathogens were Haemophilus influenza (28.0%), Moraxella catarrhalis (16.2%), and Streptococcus pneumoniae (10.2%), whereas the most common viral pathogens were rhinovirus (17.3%), influenza (12.8%), SARS-CoV-2 (11.5%), and seasonal coronaviruses (8.1%).
A study of over 3000 adults with acute cough found a prevalence of pertussis of 3%. A systematic review found prevalence of pertussis of 18% in children with at least 2 weeks of cough.

In patients taking an ACE inhibitor with a cough, it should not be assumed that the cough is always caused by the ACE inhibitor. In randomized trials, about 13.5% of patients taking an ACE reported a cough, compared with 8.5% given placebo.

A well done systematic review of 21 prevalence studies found that in Western countries, cough was caused by respiratory tract infections in 73% to 92% of patients, influenza in 6% to 15%, asthma in 3% to 15%, laryngitis/tracheitis in 4% to 9%, pneumonia in 4%, COPD in 0.5% to 3.3%, and suspected malignancy in 0.2% to 1.8%.
Cough is likely due to mucosal injury, epithelial cell damage, and the release of inflammatory mediators.
Transient airflow obstruction and transient bronchial hyperresponsiveness occur in ~40% of healthy individuals.
Reversible decline in lung function (forced expiratory volume in 1 second reduction >15%) occurs in 17% of patients.

Based on indirect evidence that Pneumococcus is a common bacterial cause of acute bronchitis or pneumonia following acute bronchitis, pneumococcal vaccine should be considered for eligible patients. C
Recommend influenza vaccine each fall to all patients at risk for complications of influenza. C
Recommend smoking cessation.C
High dose vitamin D does not reduce wintertime respiratory infections in healthy young children. B

Clinical diagnosis is based on a history of sudden onset of cough without evidence of other respiratory causes. Sputum production, either amount, color, or other characteristic should not influence diagnosis. C
Chest radiography, viral cultures, serological assays are usually not necessary, especially in patients with normal vital signs and a normal lung exam.C
Close contacts of symptomatic people with confirmed pertussis should be considered to have pertussis and should be treated. C

When clinical diagnosis remains uncertain in a high-risk patient with acute respiratory tract infection, consider using procalcitonin (PCT) to guide antibiotic initiation and cessation as this management strategy decreases mortality, antibiotic use, and antibiotic-associated adverse events regardless of the clinical setting (eg, outpatient, emergency department, inpatient, ICU). A

Differential.Differential_Features: Audible wheezes, previous history, and afebrile

list.listitem: Patients typically present with the sudden onset of cough with or without fever but without other respiratory findings. Production of sputum or presence of purulent sputum does not distinguish between pneumonia and acute bronchitis.
Patients with normal vital signs and normal lung exam have a very low likelihood of pneumonia and generally do not require radiographs or antibiotics.
Airflow obstruction may be present and may result in audible wheezes or a decrease in lung function on testing. Peak flow testing may help guide the decision to use a beta-agonist inhaler.
Patients may have their own theory as to the cause of their cough and may change their story to fit their theory. Asking patients what they think is going on may help understand their history.
Clinical examination does not distinguish viral from bacterial respiratory tract infections (LR+ 1.2; LR– 0.8).

Close contacts of a person with a confirmed or likely pertussis infection strongly suggests the same diagnosis. A cough lasting at least 2 weeks without another apparent cause, accompanied by paroxysms of cough, posttussive vomiting, or a characteristic whoop, is sufficient for a diagnosis of pertussis. A systematic review concluded that the overall clinical impression was the most accurate sign or symptom for pertussis (LR+ 3.3, LR- 0.6). Whooping (LR+ 2.1) and post-tussive vomiting (LR+ 1.7) were also helpful.
Epidemiologic outbreaks in military personnel and college students may be due to M. pneumoniae or C. pneumoniae.
Transient wheezing does not indicate asthma but may be a prominent feature in patients with underlying chronic asthma.
Patients may use the term "congestion" to include mucus or sputum in the chest.
No additional diagnostic testing usually required in adults, especially with normal lung exam and normal vital signs.

A procalcitonin (PCT) level of >2 ng/mL or a CRP level of >6.5 mg/dL may help distinguish bacterial from viral causes of RTI in children with fair sensitivity and specificity. One randomized trial set in the ED did find that PCT-guided care significantly reduced antibiotic prescribing for patients given a clinical diagnosis of acute bronchitis (17% vs 32%, NNT = 7). A Cochrane meta-analysis of 32 RCTs involving 6,708 patients with acute respiratory tract infections (ARIs) across 12 countries concluded that PCT-guided antibiotic initiation and cessation decreases mortality, antibiotic use, and antibiotic-associated adverse events regardless of clinical setting (eg, outpatient, emergency department, inpatient, ICU) or type of ARIs.

However, a second RCT of children presenting to the pediatric ED with fever or respiratory symptoms found that an 18 pathogen respiratory panel did not change antibiotic usage, ED stay, or hospitalization.
When pertussis is clinically suspected, PCR confirmation of the diagnosis using nasopharyngeal swab is recommended.
A CXR is not necessary unless a patient has one or more signs listed in .
The STARWAVe clinical prediction rule uses 7 items to predict the risk of hospitalization in children with acute cough. It has been shown to improve the accuracy of physician decision-making.
A simple 3 item risk score predicts the likellihood of pneumonia in adults with acute cough.
The GRACE prediction rule estimates the risk of pneumonia in adults with acute cough.

Clinical diagnosis is based on history of sudden onset of cough without evidence of pneumonia, common cold symptoms, acute asthma, or acute exacerbation of chronic bronchitis. Fever and sputum production may or may not be present.
CXR, viral cultures, serologic assays are not necessary unless pneumonia is clinically suspected based on abnormal lung exam or vital signs.
Treatment is symptomatic and should not involve antibiotics for most patients.
Antibiotic treatment should not be used except for those suspected to have pertussis.A
Delayed antibiotics are a safe, effective strategy for reducing inappropriate antibiotics. A
There is no good evidence supporting or refuting the effectiveness of antitussives, expectorants, mucolytics, or antihistamine-decongestant combinations in adults. B
Oral corticosteroids are not effective and should only be used if the patient has asthma or COPD exacerbation. B
Beta-agonist inhalers should not be routinely used but may be helpful in patients with wheeze accompanying cough. B
Cough suppressants should not be used in children under the age of 6 years. B

Antibiotic treatment should not be offered to patients except for those suspected to have pertussis. Antibiotic treatment is only marginally effective for adults or children with cough and RTIs that is not pneumonia, including patients with fever and green sputum. A recent study found that at best, over 4400 patients would have to be treated to prevent one episode of pneumonia.
Another study set in Africa again found no benefit, even in HIV-positive patients, of amoxicillin.

Well designed randomized trials have found that macrolide antibiotics are no more effective than vitamin C, amoxicillin, or amoxicillin-clavulanate. In a well-designed US RCT comparing azithromycin to a low dose of vitamin C, there was no difference in outcomes, including in patients with fever or purulent sputum.

Antibiotics are no more effective in smokers than nonsmokers, and may be less effective. Patients over the age of 75 years with fever; patients with COPD, heart failure, insulin-dependent diabetes; or immunocompromised patients should be considered for antibiotic treatment. Amoxicillin is first line, doxycycline is second line. The duration of treatment is 5 days.
Macrolide antibiotics should be used for adults and children with confirmed or probable whooping cough (pertussis).

For children with 4 weeks or more of "wet cough", a meta-analysis of 3 trials with 190 children concluded that antibiotics were effectively at reducing the proportion not cured at follow-up (OR 0.15, NNT = 3).
A large US observational study concluded that patients who received antibiotics had a similar duration and severity of acute LRTI than those who did not.

A delayed prescription is a good strategy for reducing antibiotic use, and are well accepted by patients. A Cochrane review found 12 studies with 3968 participants comparing immediate antibiotics, delayed antibiotics, and no antibiotics strategies for patients with acute respiratory infections. Delayed antibiotics strategy appears to decrease the rate of antibiotic use compared to immediate antibiotics and appears comparable to no antibiotics in terms of symptom control and disease complications. However, no antibiotics approach (with advice to return if symptoms do not resolve) appears to have the lowest rate of antibiotic use while maintaining comparable clinical and patient satisfaction outcomes compared to delayed prescription strategy.
Not prescribing antibiotics for children with colds or bronchitis does not increase the duration of the office visit.

A well-designed and appropriately powered RCT found no benefit from prescribing oral prednisolone (40 mg per day for 5 days) on symptom duration or severity in adults without asthma presenting for acute lower respiratory tract infection. This was even true for the subset presenting with wheezing and or shortness of breath.

There is no good evidence supporting or refuting the effectiveness of antitussives, expectorants, mucolytics, or antihistamine-decongestant combinations in adults. If patients find them helpful, they should continue using them for short-term relief.

Naproxen reduced cold symptoms in patients presenting with cough in one RCT. However, another RCT found no difference between cough duration in patients with acute bronchitis treated with ibuprofen or placebo.

Beta-agonist inhalers should not be routinely used. They do not decrease daily symptom scores or the presence of cough, night cough, or productive cough in undifferentiated patients. They may be helpful in patients with chronic asthma and patients with documented airflow obstruction or wheezing.
For patients with subacute cough (up to 8 weeks) a systematic review found no good evidence to support a clinically meaningful benefit for any drug or non-drug therapies.

A randomized trial with 194 patients compared usual care, ipratroium bromide, dextromethorphan, and honey, and found no difference between groups. The study was somewhat underpowered, but the differences were small.

Pelargonium sidoides extract (Kalwerbossie, Rabassam, Unckaloabo in Germany) reduces symptoms to a greater extent than placebo, and more patients will report satisfaction with treatment. It also allows patients to return to work on an average of 2 days faster.
Echinacea is ineffective for treating common cold symptoms.
There is insufficient evidence regarding the efficacy of Chinese herbal remedies, including Astragalus (Huang qi), for acute bronchitis.
In children, honey is more effective than no treatment, diphenhydramine, and placebo and is similar to dextromethorphan for reducing cough.
A small RCT in adults with acute bronchitis found no benefit of honey over placebo.
Giving patients an information sheet explaining acute bronchitis and the advantages and disadvantages of antibiotics will decrease antibiotic use (NNT = 8).

Referring to a patient's cough as a "chest cold" or "viral upper respiratory infection" instead of acute bronchitis may improve satisfaction with not receiving an antibiotic. When asked, only 11% of patients thought that antibiotic therapy was important to recover from "chest colds."

Delayed prescriptions (giving an antibiotic prescription but asking patient to only fill it if there is no improvement in 48 hours) has been suggested. In randomized trials, it produced similar outcomes and patient satisfaction compared to immediate antibiotic treatment. However, no antibiotics approach (with advice to return if symptoms do not resolve) appears to have the lowest rate of antibiotic use while maintaining comparable clinical and patient satisfaction outcomes compared to delayed prescription strategy.
There is no evidence for or against the recommendation to increase fluids in acute respiratory infection. Overly aggressive increase in fluids in infants or the elderly risks hyponatremia.
Cough will last about 3 weeks for the majority of patients and for at least 1 month in 25%. B
In children, 90% of respiratory infections will resolve in 3 weeks. B
In adults, about 90% of LRTI will resolve in 4 weeks.B
There is little relationship between the etiology of cough (viral or bacterial) and symptoms or duration. B

Factors predicting a serious adverse event (death, admission to hospital, pneumonia) for patients with acute LRTI include: absence of coryza, fever, chest pain, clinician-assessed severity, age >65 years, comorbidity, oxygen saturation <95%, and hypotension. B
A chest cold does not require antibiotics (use this phrase instead of "acute bronchitis").
Cough suppressants and expectorants can be tried but usually are ineffective.
The cough will last approximately 3 weeks, but may last longer in about 1 in 4 people.
Inhaled beta-agonists are US Food and Drug Administration category C in pregnancy. Oral beta-agonists should not be used because of their potential to inhibit delivery.
CXR in children with acute lower respiratory infections does not decrease subsequent visits or hospitalizations.

Cough suppressants should not be used in children under age 6 years. Cough suppressants are no more effective than placebo in children in decreasing cough or sleep when used at night, although both will decrease cough scores by more than 50%.
A Cochrane review concluded that honey is probably effective compared to diphenhydramine or no treatment, and is similar to dextromethorphan.
